ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — History and Physical — Sitting Bull — True-date frame: synthetic events are moved into the patient's historical lifetime. Codes, instruments, and treatments remain modern and are anachronistic.

code.originalText: Establishing care at the clinic for chronic pain in the left ankle and hindfoot with a limp after an old gunshot wound: a culturally safe, trauma-informed history, X-rays, screening for diabetes, high blood pressure and depression, and food

text.paragraph: Establishing care at the clinic for chronic pain in the left ankle and hindfoot with a limp after an old gunshot wound: a culturally safe, trauma-informed history, X-rays, screening for diabetes, high blood pressure and depression, and food [S]
This fictional modern episode addresses the presenting concerns below. [S]

list.item: He wants to walk his land and ride without pain, and does not want his foot cut open unless there is no other way. [S]
He wants care that respects who he is and his own ways of healing. [S]
His family does not have enough food at the end of the month. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Sitting Bull was born in the early 1830s, between 1831 and 1837 by the reckoning of different sources, into a prominent Hunkpapa Lakota family near the Grand River in present-day South Dakota, at a place called Many Caches. [D]

His boyhood name was Jumping Badger, and he was called Slow for his deliberate ways; as a young man he received his father's name, Tȟatȟáŋka Íyotake (Sitting Bull), also written Tatanka Iyotake or Tatanka-Iyotanka. [D]

He became a leading Hunkpapa warrior, hunter and leader, admitted to respected warrior societies, and by about 1866 or 1867 was recognized as an important political and military leader of the Lakota bands resisting encroachment on their lands. [D]

He was also a holy man, a wichasha wakan (in the modern Lakota orthography wičháša wakȟáŋ), whose calling was confirmed in the Sun Dance; historians note that equating a wichasha wakan with a medicine man is misleading. [D]

In a fight with Crow warriors, about 1856 by his biographer's account, he was shot in the foot: the Crow chief's shot struck his shield and then cut a groove along his foot from heel to toe. The wound troubled him for the rest of his life and left him with a limp. [D]
In 1864 he was again wounded, through the hip and back, in an attack on a wagon train crossing Lakota territory. [D]

In June 1876, before the battle at the Little Bighorn (the Greasy Grass), he led a Sun Dance on Rosebud Creek, offering fifty pieces of flesh from each arm and fasting, and had a vision of soldiers falling into the camp; his village was attacked later that month, and he, beyond fighting age, did not fight himself. [D]
After the battle the army pursued the Lakota bands, and in 1877 he led his people north into Canada, where the buffalo were scarce, food was short, sickness spread and the winters were hard. [D]

Starving, he and the remaining Hunkpapa surrendered at Fort Buford, Dakota Territory, on July 20, 1881; despite promises that they would go to Standing Rock, he and his followers were held as prisoners of war at Fort Randall for nearly two years. [D]

In May 1883 he was allowed to join his people at the Standing Rock Reservation, where there were too few bison to support the Hunkpapa, he was sent to work in the farm fields, and he chose to live in a cabin on the Grand River near where he was born. [D]
He toured with Wild West shows in 1884 and 1885, spending four months of 1885 with William F. Cody's show, and then returned to Standing Rock, where the agent would not let him rejoin the show. [D]

list.item: Hunkpapa Lakota; a respected leader and holy man of his people; lives with his family in a log house on the Grand River near where he was born, on the Standing Rock Reservation, about an hour's drive from the clinic; keeps horses and a garden [S]
Speaks Lakota as his first language and some English; chose to have the clinic's Lakota-speaking interpreter at his visits; asked to be called Sitting Bull [S]

His people's way of life was taken from them within his lifetime: the buffalo are gone, the bands were pursued and exiled, he was held as a prisoner, and his people now farm and depend on government food; he spoke of these losses plainly and chose not to discuss them further at the first visit [S]
Diet: commodity foods (flour, canned meat, lard, sugar, coffee), garden vegetables in season and game when it can be found; food runs short at the end of each month [S]
Does not drink alcohol; does not use commercial tobacco (traditional and ceremonial use was not asked about and is not recorded) [S]

Traditional healing: he has his own spiritual practices and healers and will decide whether and how they are part of his care; the clinic offered access through its traditional medicine program and asked nothing further [S]

Strengths and supports: his standing and responsibilities among his people, a deep spiritual life, decades of endurance, family around him, horsemanship, and a clear sense of what he wants from care [S]

Culturally safe, trauma-informed care: ask how he wishes to be addressed and what matters to him, offer the Lakota interpreter, take time, explain each examination and ask consent first, and do not probe his history or beliefs beyond what he chooses to share. Guideline: Indian Health Manual, Part 3, Chapter 30: Chronic Non-Cancer Pain Management (2026); Special General Memorandum 94-08: Statement of Policy for the Traditional Cultural Advocacy Program (1994) [S]

Orthopaedic foot and ankle consultation at the clinic's visiting specialist session to confirm the diagnosis and explain every treatment option, including surgery. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026) [S]

Imaging: weight-bearing X-rays today; CT if they show arthritis or metal, to map the joints and any fragments; blood lead only if fragments are found, since fragments in a joint or bone raise lead levels. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); Lead toxicity from retained bullet fragments: A systematic review and meta-analysis (2019) [S]

Pain: diclofenac gel first; an oral NSAID for a limited time only after home blood pressure and kidney function are checked; acetaminophen if needed; no opioids, which the Indian Health Service advises against as an initial treatment for chronic pain. Guideline: 2019 American College of Rheumatology/Arthritis Foundation Guideline for the Management of Osteoarthritis of the Hand, Hip, and Knee (2019); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026); Indian Health Manual, Part 3, Chapter 30: Chronic Non-Cancer Pain Management (2026) [S]

Prediabetes: walking and riding as the foot allows, fewer refined foods and more vegetables and traditional foods, the clinic's diabetes prevention program funded by the Special Diabetes Program for Indians, and hemoglobin A1c again in three to four months. Guideline: Special Diabetes Program for Indians (2026); Prediabetes and Type 2 Diabetes: Screening (2021) [S]

Blood pressure: home readings twice daily for a week with a clinic monitor before the next visit, since one raised clinic reading does not make a diagnosis. Guideline: Hypertension in Adults: Screening (2021); 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults (2025) [S]

Emotional well-being: depression screening with the PHQ-2 and PHQ-9; grief and anger about real losses are not treated as a disorder; behavioral health and traditional healing are available whenever he chooses, side by side with clinic care. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis and depression, bipolar, and mood disorders monographs (2026); Special General Memorandum 94-08: Statement of Policy for the Traditional Cultural Advocacy Program (1994); Depression and Suicide Risk in Adults: Screening (2023) [S]

Food: the Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (which offers bison and other traditional foods) or SNAP, garden support, and the Community Health Representative to help with forms. Guideline: Community Health Representative Program (2026); Food Distribution Program on Indian Reservations (2026) [S]
